title: From a Bloated Curriculum to Instructional Coherence
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Samantha Lippert, a third-grade teacher in a small rural district, explains how she turned the McGraw Hill Wonders materials from a sprawling set of components into a coherent, knowledge-building approach. Her starting point is that high-quality materials are not the same as high-quality instruction: students reading "Sailing to America" lack the background to understand immigration, so she builds that knowledge first. She annotates the core text to identify the knowledge, vocabulary and language it demands, then makes the text the organizing center for every other component. Fluency passages are rewritten to carry target vocabulary, vocabulary is taught in contrasting pairs with attention to spelling and orthographic mapping, and grammar becomes sentence-expansion work drawn from The Writing Revolution. She presents this as a method any teacher can apply to whatever curriculum is in front of them, without lowering expectations or abandoning the texts.
points: Start with the text, not the lesson plan: annotate what a student must know to comprehend it, then plan backward from those demands.
Make the core text the organizing center so that fluency, vocabulary, grammar and writing all reinforce the same knowledge.
Custom fluency passages that carry the target vocabulary let a few minutes of practice build both automaticity and knowledge.
Teach vocabulary in contrasting pairs and connect pronunciation, spelling and meaning, drawing on Ehri's orthographic mapping.
Sentence expansion (kernel sentence plus why, where, who) ties grammar to content and shows the skill gap between "The family went to America" and a fully developed sentence.
quotes: This is one of the instructional challenges that can emerge when we mistake the presence of high-quality instructional materials for the presence of high-quality instruction.
We are asking students to comprehend something they don’t yet have the knowledge to comprehend.
I didn’t want to abandon the texts. I didn’t want to lower expectations. I didn’t want to replace the curriculum with something entirely different.

The core text became the organizing center of my instruction. Instead of asking how to fit every curriculum component into the week, I now ask how each component can contribute to my students’ understanding of that text and its ideas.
Fluency instruction is no longer an isolated activity. It has become another opportunity to reinforce what students are learning.
Orthographic mapping involves connecting a word’s spelling, pronunciation, and meaning so that it can be stored and recognized automatically.

The goal is not simply for students to be able to define immigrated. It is for them to understand the word well enough to recognize it, explain it, and use it when discussing the experiences of the families in the texts.
Students are not simply adding words to make a sentence longer. They are thinking about the relationship between ideas, using vocabulary from the text set, and communicating what they understand.
